article_title: Amazon's Zoox Recalls 105 Robotaxis After One Drove Into Heavy Smoke at an Active Fire Scene
summary: Substantively accurate and well-sourced; publishing with one correction because the 'over-the-air' delivery characterization is not supported by any cited source.

findings.message: The article describes the fix as an "over-the-air" software update in both the summary and the body, attributing the characterization to TechCrunch, but none of the four cited sources use the phrase 'over-the-air' or otherwise specify the update's delivery method.
findings.details: TechCrunch says Zoox 'shipped to its fleet of 105 vehicles a software update'; Gizmodo says the company 'released a software update to all affected vehicles'; Engadget says Zoox is 'rolling out' the update; Futurism describes it as a fix 'in the form of a software update.' The event (a software recall fixed via software update) is fully sourced; only the 'over-the-air' delivery descriptor is unsupported. This is a single recoverable issue honestly covered by a corrections record, not a fabricated event, so the verdict is APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS rather than REJECT.

content_preview.title: Amazon's Zoox Recalls 105 Robotaxis After One Drove Into Heavy Smoke at an Active Fire Scene
content_preview.summary: Amazon-owned Zoox is recalling software across its 105-robotaxi fleet after a driverless car entered heavy smoke at an uncordoned fire scene on June 20, fixing the flaw with an over-the-air update.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Amazon-owned Zoox is recalling the software that runs its entire fleet of 105 robotaxis after one of the driverless cars entered heavy smoke at an active fire scene and failed to respond as intended, according to [Futurism](https://futurism.com/advanced-transport/amazon-robotaxi-confused-smoke-recall). Zoox recalled the software across the fleet over concerns the vehicles "may fail to properly detect and respond to heavy smoke," [Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/zoox-issues-recall-after...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean, well-structured News piece (422 words, within the 400-1200 News range). Clear Overview/What Happened/The Fix/Context sections, neutral throughout, no AI self-reference, no editorializing. Every paragraph attributes its claims to a named outlet.
editor_notes.source_verification: I personally decompressed and read all four committed snapshots. source-0.html.gz (TechCrunch): confirms fleet of 105 vehicles, June 20 incident with heavy smoke obscuring an active emergency fire scene 'not cordoned off with cones', 'Nobody was on board', 'not aware of injuries', July 17 2026 report date (Sean O'Kane), and the verbatim location non-disclosure quote 'The NHTSA's report doesn't state where the June incident took place, and Zoox declined to say.' The NHTSA campaign number 26E044000 is genuinely supported: it appears in the source's embedded NHTSA recall hyperlink (href https://www.nhtsa.gov/?nhtsaId=26E044000) in BOTH TechCrunch and Engadget, so the attribution 'campaign number 26E044000, according to TechCrunch' is accurate. source-1.html.gz (Engadget): verbatim quotes confirmed — 'The Zoox vehicle entered the scene, then braked hard while attempting to steer away before coming to a stop', 'under a teleguidance tactician's guidance, reversed', 'placed traffic cones at the scene blocking two of the three through-lanes', and the May 2025 Las Vegas passenger-car collision recall. source-2.html.gz (Gizmodo): verbatim 'may fail to properly detect and respond to heavy smoke', the full Zoox spokesperson root-cause quote ('detecting active EV scenes ... heavy smoke in certain situations'), the free-rides-in-Las-Vegas-and-San-Francisco / testing-in-Austin-and-Miami context, and the earlier-recalls list (hard braking, lane crossing, failing to predict movement of nearby cars). source-3.html.gz (Futurism): confirms the Amazon-owned framing and 'entire fleet of 105 autonomous robotaxis'. The one claim I could NOT verify in any source (0 occurrences across all four raw snapshots): the phrase 'over-the-air'.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All specifics verified against sources except the 'over-the-air' delivery descriptor. Fleet size (105), incident date (June 20), report date (July 17), the NHTSA campaign number, all direct quotes, and the prior-recall history are accurate. Critically, the article does NOT assert a location for the June 20 incident — it explicitly states neither the company nor the regulator disclosed where it occurred and quotes TechCrunch to that effect. The Las Vegas references are correctly scoped to (a) Zoox's general operations and (b) the separate May 2025 collision recall, neither of which is the June smoke incident. No aggregator 'Las Vegas' error is repeated.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and factual. No sensationalism, no loaded language, appropriate for a News category recall story.
editor_notes.originality: New topic. No prior Machine Herald article covers the Zoox smoke recall. The only prior Zoox mention is a March 2026 Uber-robotaxi-deals piece (different subject). The internal cross-reference to the March 2026 Waymo/first-responders article resolves to an existing published article.
concerns: The word 'over-the-air' in the summary and 'The Fix' section is attributed to TechCrunch but does not appear in any of the four cited sources, which describe the fix only as a software update shipped/rolled out/released to the fleet. Filed as a public correction; the article publishes with the corrections trail attached.
recommendations: When characterizing an update's delivery mechanism, use only wording the cited source supports (e.g., 'a software update shipped to its fleet') unless a source explicitly states it is over-the-air.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively accurate, well-sourced, neutral News piece. The single recoverable issue (the unsupported 'over-the-air' characterization attributed to TechCrunch) is honestly covered by a corrections record, so the article publishes under APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS rather than being rejected.
